name: Relative afferent pupillary defect
presentation: Both pupils are the same size and both constrict when a light is shone in either eye, but when the light is swung quickly from the good eye to the bad eye, the bad eye's pupil dilates instead of staying small, and when swung back to the good eye both constrict again. This paradoxical dilation is the relative afferent pupillary defect, the most reliable objective sign of a unilateral or asymmetric optic nerve lesion, present even when acuity is normal.

deficits.sign: Paradoxical dilation of the affected pupil on the swinging flashlight test; no anisocoria
Usually reduced acuity, color desaturation or a field defect in the same eye
With an optic tract lesion, the RAPD is in the eye with the temporal field loss, contralateral to the lesion

reasoning: The light reflex has a bilateral afferent input and a bilateral efferent output: light in one eye drives both pretectal nuclei through the crossed and uncrossed fibers of the chiasm, and each pretectal nucleus drives both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, so the direct and consensual responses are normally equal and the two pupils are always the same size. A lesion of one optic nerve reduces the signal from that eye but not the response of either pupil to the other eye, so the pupils remain equal, and the only way to expose the deficit is to compare the two afferent inputs directly by alternating the light between the eyes: when the light moves to the damaged eye the total drive to the pupils falls and both pupils dilate, which the examiner sees in the illuminated eye. This is why an RAPD never causes anisocoria, why it is graded by comparison rather than measured in absolute terms, and why it cannot be detected when both nerves are equally affected. Because the crossing nasal fibers outnumber the uncrossed temporal fibers, a lesion of one optic tract, which contains the crossed fibers of the contralateral eye and the uncrossed fibers of the ipsilateral eye, reduces the input from the contralateral eye more and produces a small RAPD in the eye opposite the lesion, together with a homonymous hemianopia. Lesions beyond the geniculate spare the pupil, so a hemianopia with an RAPD is a tract lesion. Dense cataract, corneal opacity or media disease do not produce an RAPD, since the light scattered through them still reaches the retina.

imagingFindings.finding: Enhancing segment of the optic nerve on fat-suppressed orbital images.
Meningioma, glioma or orbital mass along the nerve; canal narrowing on CT.
Lesion of the tract lateral to the hypothalamus with a contralateral hemianopia.

commonCauses: Large retinal detachment or central retinal artery or vein occlusion

mimics.name: Hippus
mimics.howToDistinguish: Rhythmic oscillation of both pupils unrelated to the side of illumination

mimics.name: Anisocoria of any cause
mimics.howToDistinguish: An efferent problem; the RAPD test compares constriction, not size

management: Perform the swinging flashlight test in every patient with unexplained visual loss or a suspected optic neuropathy
An RAPD with normal acuity and fundus still requires optic nerve imaging
Grade with neutral density filters when quantification is needed

imagingHint.label: optic nerve from the globe to the chiasm
